title: When Does Storage Complement Solar? Investment and Cost Recovery under Advanced Net Metering

paper.title: When Does Storage Complement Solar? Investment and Cost Recovery under Advanced Net Metering
paper.abstract:
Abstract We examine the joint PV and storage operational and investment decisions of a prosumer under net energy metering (NEM) and peak/off-peak tariffs (ToU). Legacy NEM compensates net exports at the retail rate over a netting period, typically under time-invariant pricing. To better reflect system costs, tariff features are being reconsidered, with many U.S. states adopting time-varying prices and export compensation below the retail price.
We formulate the prosumer decision problem as a cost minimization problem with charge/discharge, PV investment, and storage investment decisions. We analytically derive the optimal decisions based on the tariff’s membership in one of six regions that partition the tariff space. Using these solutions, we examine the relationship between PV and storage, identifying when they are complements or substitutes . Furthermore, we identify the relationship between private DER incentives and the distribution utility’s (DU’s) net cost of serving the prosumer. For both storage and PV, when investment costs are greater than the costs of serving the customer, there is no tariff where investment in PV and storage decrease non-adopter bills. Under the same conditions, complementarity between PV and storage decreases DU cost recovery for a given tariff. In a Massachusetts-based case study, we validate our theoretical findings by connecting tariff design features to DER interaction, the DU’s net cost, and DER adoption in a stochastic, multi-prosumer, and multi-period setting.

sections.heading: I Introduction
sections.text: The rapid deployment of behind-the-meter (BTM) distributed energy resources (DERs), particularly rooftop photovoltaic (PV) systems, is transforming electricity consumption and generation patterns at the distribution level. Consumers equipped with such resources, termed prosumers, are able to both import electricity from and export surplus generation to the distribution utility (DU) [ 6 ] . Net energy metering (NEM) has emerged as the predominant tariff mechanism for facilitating bidirectional energy exchange in the United States. Under conventional NEM, a prosumer’s net energy consumption is calculated over a netting period. Net imports are charged at the retail price and net exports are compensated with credits, traditionally valued near the retail rate (symmetric NEM) or at a reduced price (asymmetric NEM) [ 16 ] 1 1 1 Symmetric and asymmetric NEM designs are also referred to in the literature as full NEM and partial NEM (or net billing), respectively. . Legacy NEM tariffs are often implemented in conjunction with time-invariant (TI) volumetric tariffs. This means that residential prosumers are charged the same per $/kWh rate no matter the time of day (time-invariance) or whether they are net-producers or consumers (symmetric NEM). Both TI pricing and symmetric NEM cause distortions to the price of electricity as they do not accurately convey the costs of supplying prosumers with electricity. TI pricing does not represent the actual cost of producing electricity in a particular time period. Symmetric NEM increases this distortion when export compensation exceeds the costs that the grid avoids from receiving that electricity. A second problem of volumetric tariffs that is exacerbated by NEM is the recovery of fixed costs. Since fixed and per kW costs are being recovered through a per kWh charge, NEM not only lets the prosumer avoid the per kWh charge, it can also reduce their contribution to costs that do not decrease proportionally with their net purchases [ 13 ] . We focus on NEM tariffs because their import and export prices determine the private value of PV generation, and how storage changes these values. Although many existing NEM tariffs remain TI and symmetric, a growing number of jurisdictions are transitioning toward time-varying and asymmetric import/export tariff structures. Notable examples of asymmetric NEM tariffs include those adopted in California, Arizona, Georgia, Michigan, and Illinois [ 15 ] . These reforms aim to align customer incentives with system costs [ 4 , 1 ] . Lowering the export rate reduces over-compensation when export credits exceed avoided system costs. Similarly, shifting from a TI tariff to a time-of-use (ToU) tariff brings exposes the customers to a tariff that better reflects variation in system costs. Here, we examine a tariff with peak and off-peak periods, the simplest ToU schedule. Asymmetric NEM and ToU can also encourage prosumers to pair storage with PV. When export compensation is below the retail price, storing surplus PV generation for later consumption can increase the private value of solar electricity. ToU prices also increase storage profitability since low-cost grid or stored solar generation displaces purchases during higher-priced periods. Due to this interaction, ToU tariffs are perceived as encouraging adoption of combined PV and storage systems [ 18 ] and peak reduction that provides both private and system benefits [ 22 ] . These potential benefits also motivate policy recommendations to use time-varying retail rates to compensate the system value of combinations of DERs [ 19 ] . However, the conditions under which PV and storage act as complements or substitutes under a NEM and whether it is possible to find an NEM tariff which reduces non-adopter bills while recovering costs have not been addressed (to the best of our knowledge). Much of the existing literature on NEM examines the problem through an econometric analysis of consumers and prosumers using historical data or by examining prosumer decision-making as an optimization problem, although there is overlap. In the first category, early work studies prosumer benefits, net demand, and PV adoption under legacy NEM tariffs with symmetric prices [ 5 , 10 , 21 ] . Other work examines the effect of NEM on bill savings, cost shifts to non-adopting consumers, and the overall efficiency of NEM tariffs [ 6 ] . Another line of work within this category endogenizes the PV capacity under NEM, but abstracts from storage operation [ 9 , 7 ] . These works highlight the distributional and revenue-adequacy consequences of volumetric cost recovery when customers can adopt BTM generation but without considering the endogenous storage adoption. In the second category of literature, operational decisions and DER aggregation are presented as an optimization under time-varying and asymmetric NEM tariffs [ 2 , 8 ] , but generally maintain the assumption of exogenous PV capacity. A separate line of work endogenizes the PV capacity under NEM, but abstracts from demand flexibility and storage operation [ 9 , 3 , 7 ] . Related literature studies how tariff design, DER adoption, and utility cost recovery interact at the aggregate level, while keeping DER adoption decisions fairly abstract [ 20 ] . Our work is in the second category. We extend the literature on prosumer behavior and examine its implications for retail tariff design in order to address problems with NEM described by the first literature category. Specifically, we characterize how a prosumer jointly optimizes operational decisions, PV investment, and storage investment under a potentially asymmetric NEM tariff with peak and off-peak periods. We show when PV and storage are complements or substitutes under this tariff structure, and how these decisions impact the regulator tariff design problem.

sections.heading: Summary of Contributions:
sections.text: This paper first studies the joint optimal investment and operational decisions of a prosumer with BTM PV generation and battery storage under ToU-NEM tariffs. In particular, the paper makes the following contributions: • Optimal Decisions and Price Regions: We identify six regions that partition the ToU-NEM tariff space and show how optimal storage operation and investment is determined based upon tariff location within these regions. • Complementarity/Substitutability: We show that PV and storage act as complements or substitutes based on three factors: (1) whether storage causes a crossing of the net zero boundary, (2) the distribution of PV capacity factor, and (3) import/export price differences. • DER interaction and cost recovery: We provide sufficient conditions for when DERs increase DU costs. We then establish the two roles complementarity plays in tariff design: increasing DU costs and increasing PV investment. In summary, the main contribution of our work is to examine the interaction the joint investment of PV and storage operational connect this to the regulator’s tariff design problem. The paper proceeds as follows. Section II formulates the NEM tariff and the prosumer problem. Section III characterizes battery operations, PV investment, and storage investment decisions under the tariff. Section IV analyzes the DU net-cost effect of PV and storage adoption. Section V presents a Massachusetts-based case study, and Section VI concludes. Formal proofs are provided in the appendix in [ 11 ] .

sections.text: We conduct a case study using a population of 500 Massachusetts single-family homes under NEM. sections.heading: VI Conclusion
sections.text: This paper characterizes the optimal joint investment and operational decisions of a prosumer who can invest in BTM PV and storage under a NEM tariff with peak and off-peak prices. From these optimal decisions, we isolate the factors that cause PV and storage to act as complements or substitutes and examine the implications for DU cost recovery. PV and storage are complements when storage increases PV value in the off-peak more than it decreases PV marginal value in the peak. The three factors that contribute to this are the ratio of capacity factors in the peak and off-peak, the export-import price spread in each period, and DER capacities. Higher off-peak capacity factors and price spreads contribute to complementarity, while those same factors contribute to substitution during the peak. Each effect can only exist when there are PV and storage capacities capable of reaching the net net-zero exchange threshold in either period. This understanding of DER interaction has implications for the cost recovery and decarbonization dilemma faced by regulators as DERs become cheaper and more widespread. Under a complementarity inducing tariff, storage can increase the cost shifts caused by PV. At the same time, complementarity can increase the penetration of PV and contribute to the decarbonization of the electricity grid. These findings suggest that regulators should evaluate PV and storage jointly. Policies that promote co-adoption can support PV deployment while increasing DU revenue shortfalls. However, tariffs that would previously not be considered do to their negative effect on PV could provide an appropriate balance between balancing costs and PV adoption. Conversely, storage that displaces PV can improve cost recovery while reducing PV deployment. These outcomes depend on the timing of import-export price asymmetries and prevailing technology costs. Tariff design should therefore weigh storage’s effect on PV investment alongside its operational benefits, balancing decarbonization objectives with utility cost recovery.

The full paper, including proofs of theoretical results, is available in [ 11 ] . A preliminary version of this paper was published as a conference paper at the PowerUp Conference, Boulder, CO, 2026 [ 12 ] . Abstract We examine the joint PV and storage operational and investment decisions of a prosumer under net energy metering (NEM) and peak/off-peak tariffs (ToU). Legacy NEM compensates net exports at the retail rate over a netting period, typically under time-invariant pricing. To better reflect system costs, tariff features are being reconsidered, with many U.S. states adopting time-varying prices and export compensation below the retail price. We formulate the prosumer decision problem as a cost minimization problem with charge/discharge, PV investment, and storage investment decisions. We analytically derive the optimal decisions based on the tariff’s membership in one of six regions that partition the tariff space. Using these solutions, we examine the relationship between PV and storage, identifying when they are complements or substitutes . Furthermore, we identify the relationship between private DER incentives and the distribution utility’s (DU’s) net cost of serving the prosumer. For both storage and PV, when investment costs are greater than the costs of serving the customer, there is no tariff where investment in PV and storage decrease non-adopter bills. Under the same conditions, complementarity between PV and storage decreases DU cost recovery for a given tariff. In a Massachusetts-based case study, we validate our theoretical findings by connecting tariff design features to DER interaction, the DU’s net cost, and DER adoption in a stochastic, multi-prosumer, and multi-period setting. Index Terms: Batteries, cost recovery, distributed energy resources, net metering, prosumers, solar PV, tariff design. I Introduction The rapid deployment of behind-the-meter (BTM) distributed energy resources (DERs), particularly rooftop photovoltaic (PV) systems, is transforming electricity consumption and generation patterns at the distribution level. Consumers equipped with such resources, termed prosumers, are able to both import electricity from and export surplus generation to the distribution utility (DU) [ 6 ] . Net energy metering (NEM) has emerged as the predominant tariff mechanism for facilitating bidirectional energy exchange in the United States. Under conventional NEM, a prosumer’s net energy consumption is calculated over a netting period. Net imports are charged at the retail price and net exports are compensated with credits, traditionally valued near the retail rate (symmetric NEM) or at a reduced price (asymmetric NEM) [ 16 ] 1 1 1 Symmetric and asymmetric NEM designs are also referred to in the literature as full NEM and partial NEM (or net billing), respectively. . Legacy NEM tariffs are often implemented in conjunction with time-invariant (TI) volumetric tariffs. This means that residential prosumers are charged the same per $/kWh rate no matter the time of day (time-invariance) or whether they are net-producers or consumers (symmetric NEM). Both TI pricing and symmetric NEM cause distortions to the price of electricity as they do not accurately convey the costs of supplying prosumers with electricity. TI pricing does not represent the actual cost of producing electricity in a particular time period. Symmetric NEM increases this distortion when export compensation exceeds the costs that the grid avoids from receiving that electricity. A second problem of volumetric tariffs that is exacerbated by NEM is the recovery of fixed costs. Since fixed and per kW costs are being recovered through a per kWh charge, NEM not only lets the prosumer avoid the per kWh charge, it can also reduce their contribution to costs that do not decrease proportionally with their net purchases [ 13 ] . We focus on NEM tariffs because their import and export prices determine the private value of PV generation, and how storage changes these values. Although many existing NEM tariffs remain TI and symmetric, a growing number of jurisdictions are transitioning toward time-varying and asymmetric import/export tariff structures. Notable examples of asymmetric NEM tariffs include those adopted in California, Arizona, Georgia, Michigan, and Illinois [ 15 ] . These reforms aim to align customer incentives with system costs [ 4 , 1 ] . Lowering the export rate reduces over-compensation when export credits exceed avoided system costs. Similarly, shifting from a TI tariff to a time-of-use (ToU) tariff brings exposes the customers to a tariff that better reflects variation in system costs. Here, we examine a tariff with peak and off-peak periods, the simplest ToU schedule. Asymmetric NEM and ToU can also encourage prosumers to pair storage with PV. When export compensation is below the retail price, storing surplus PV generation for later consumption can increase the private value of solar electricity. ToU prices also increase storage profitability since low-cost grid or stored solar generation displaces purchases during higher-priced periods. Due to this interaction, ToU tariffs are perceived as encouraging adoption of combined PV and storage systems [ 18 ] and peak reduction that provides both private and system benefits [ 22 ] . These potential benefits also motivate policy recommendations to use time-varying retail rates to compensate the system value of combinations of DERs [ 19 ] . However, the conditions under which PV and storage act as complements or substitutes under a NEM and whether it is possible to find an NEM tariff which reduces non-adopter bills while recovering costs have not been addressed (to the best of our knowledge). Much of the existing literature on NEM examines the problem through an econometric analysis of consumers and prosumers using historical data or by examining prosumer decision-making as an optimization problem, although there is overlap. In the first category, early work studies prosumer benefits, net demand, and PV adoption under legacy NEM tariffs with symmetric prices [ 5 , 10 , 21 ] . Other work examines the effect of NEM on bill savings, cost shifts to non-adopting consumers, and the overall efficiency of NEM tariffs [ 6 ] . Another line of work within this category endogenizes the PV capacity under NEM, but abstracts from storage operation [ 9 , 7 ] . These works highlight the distributional and revenue-adequacy consequences of volumetric cost recovery when customers can adopt BTM generation but without considering the endogenous storage adoption. In the second category of literature, operational decisions and DER aggregation are presented as an optimization under time-varying and asymmetric NEM tariffs [ 2 , 8 ] , but generally maintain the assumption of exogenous PV capacity. A separate line of work endogenizes the PV capacity under NEM, but abstracts from demand flexibility and storage operation [ 9 , 3 , 7 ] . Related literature studies how tariff design, DER adoption, and utility cost recovery interact at the aggregate level, while keeping DER adoption decisions fairly abstract [ 20 ] . Our work is in the second category. We extend the literature on prosumer behavior and examine its implications for retail tariff design in order to address problems with NEM described by the first literature category. Specifically, we characterize how a prosumer jointly optimizes operational decisions, PV investment, and storage investment under a potentially asymmetric NEM tariff with peak and off-peak periods. We show when PV and storage are complements or substitutes under this tariff structure, and how these decisions impact the regulator tariff design problem. Summary of Contributions: This paper first studies the joint optimal investment and operational decisions of a prosumer with BTM PV generation and battery storage under ToU-NEM tariffs. In particular, the paper makes the following contributions: • Optimal Decisions and Price Regions: We identify six regions that partition the ToU-NEM tariff space and show how optimal storage operation and investment is determined based upon tariff location within these regions. • Complementarity/Substitutability: We show that PV and storage act as complements or substitutes based on three factors: (1) whether storage causes a crossing of the net zero boundary, (2) the distribution of PV capacity factor, and (3) import/export price differences. • DER interaction and cost recovery: We provide sufficient conditions for when DERs increase DU costs.
